title: CIA, AAA, and Non-Repudiation: The Principles That Underpin Everything Else

blocks.text: Before tools, there are three questions: is information protected, can we know who did what, and can we prove it? All of security rests on these answers.
The CIA Triad
**Confidentiality**: only authorized individuals can access information. It is ensured through encryption, access control, classification, and segmentation.
**Integrity**: information is neither modified nor altered in an undetected manner. It is ensured through hashing, signatures, version controls, and tamper-evident logs.
**Availability**: information and services are accessible when needed. It is ensured through redundancy, backups, denial-of-service protection, and proper capacity planning.

blocks.title: The Classic Trap
blocks.text: Encrypting a disk protects **confidentiality**, not availability. Ransomware attacks **availability** by encrypting data: here, encryption becomes the weapon, not the defense. Always read the question by asking yourself **which pillar is targeted**.
AAA: Authentication, Authorization, Accounting

**Authentication** answers "who are you?". **Authorization** answers "do you have permission?". **Accounting** (or auditing) answers "what did you do?". The order matters: you cannot authorize without having authenticated, nor trace without having identified.

blocks.field: Often referred to as the "AAA framework". Do not confuse it with the AAA network protocol (RADIUS, TACACS+) that implements these three functions.

blocks.text: Non-Repudiation

**Non-repudiation** ensures that a party cannot deny having performed an action. It relies on proof verifiable by a third party: digital signature with a private key, reliable timestamping, integrity-protected logging. A simple shared password proves nothing: anyone with the password could have acted.

blocks.field: In practice: qualified electronic signature, timestamping, write-once audit log. Non-repudiation is as much a **legal** requirement as a technical one.

blocks.title: Signing ≠ Encrypting
blocks.text: You **sign** with your private key to prove origin (authenticity, integrity, non-repudiation). You **encrypt** with the recipient's public key to protect confidentiality. Both operations can coexist on the same message.
Least Privilege and Separation of Duties

**Least privilege** consists of giving each identity the minimum access necessary, for the duration necessary. **Separation of duties** prevents a single person from carrying out a critical action end-to-end: requesting, approving, and paying an expense, or developing and deploying to production without review.

blocks.q: A ransomware attack encrypts a service's files and makes them inaccessible. Which pillar is primarily affected?
options: Confidentiality, because the data is encrypted
Availability, because the data is no longer accessible
Integrity, because the files have changed
Non-repudiation, because we don't know who encrypted them
blocks.explain: Ransomware uses encryption as a weapon, but the intended effect is unavailability. Integrity is also affected, but the goal of the attack is to block access to extort a payment.

items: CIA: confidentiality, integrity, availability — three distinct pillars, three control families.
AAA: authenticate, authorize, account — in that order.
Non-repudiation requires third-party verifiable proof, not just a local log.
Least privilege and separation of duties reduce the blast radius of a compromised account.

title: Defense in Depth and Zero Trust: Two Answers to the Same Question

blocks.text: No control is infallible. Defense in depth bets on layering; Zero Trust bets on continuous verification. Both are tested on the exam, and they are not mutually exclusive.
Defense in Depth

**Defense in depth** stacks independent controls so that a single failure is not enough to compromise the asset. A user clicks a link: the email filter could have blocked it, EDR can stop execution, segmentation limits lateral movement, and backups enable recovery.

Depth is not the number of products. Three antivirus programs on the same workstation do not constitute defense in depth: they cover the same layer and the same failure mode. Depth comes from **layer diversity**: perimeter, network, host, application, data, identity, human, physical.

items: **Perimeter**: firewall, web gateway, email filtering.
**Network**: segmentation, IDS/IPS, network access control (NAC).
**Host**: hardening, EDR, application control.
**Application**: input validation, authentication, static analysis.
**Data**: classification, encryption, DLP, backups.
**Identity**: MFA, least privilege, access reviews.
**Human**: awareness training, procedures, separation of duties.
**Physical**: badge, mantrap, video surveillance.

blocks.text: Zero Trust

**Zero Trust** starts from the principle that no network zone is trustworthy by default, including the internal network. Every access is verified based on context: identity, device, application, data sensitivity, behavior. The slogan "never trust, always verify" sums up the idea; "assume breach" follows from it: you design as if the attacker is already inside.

left.title: Traditional Perimeter Approach
points: Verification at entry, then implicit trust
Easy lateral movement once the perimeter is breached
VPN = broad access to the network

right.title: Zero Trust
points: Verification on every request, based on context
Microsegmentation and application-level access, not network-level

blocks.title: Zero Trust Is Not a Product
blocks.text: You don't "deploy" Zero Trust by buying an appliance. It is an **architecture**: identity policy, device inventory, segmentation, logging, strong authentication. A vendor claiming to sell "the Zero Trust solution" is selling a building block, not the architecture.

The Zero Trust principles expected on the exam: verify explicitly, use least privilege, assume breach, continuously authenticate and authorize, segment access by application, and log every decision for auditing.

blocks.q: A company adds a second antivirus to its workstations. Is this an improvement to defense in depth?
options: Yes: two controls are better than one
No: both controls cover the same layer and the same failure mode
Yes, provided the two vendors are different
No: antivirus is never a security control
blocks.explain: Defense in depth relies on layer diversity. Two antivirus programs on the same host add little extra depth, can interfere with each other, and increase overhead. The question to ask is: what failure mode does this new control cover that the previous one does not?

items: Defense in depth = **diverse** layers, not stacking identical products.
Zero Trust = no implicit trust, continuous contextual verification.
Microsegmentation and ZTNA replace the "trusted intranet + broad VPN" model.
Both approaches complement each other: depth of controls, zero trust in access.

title: Control Categories and Types: The Matrix to Know by Heart

blocks.text: The exam doesn't just ask you to name a control: it asks you to classify it. A single control has a category (how it acts) and a type (when and why it acts).

The **category** describes the nature of the control: technical/logical, managerial/administrative, physical/environmental, operational. The **type** describes its function over time: preventive, deterrent, corrective, detective, compensating, directive.

blocks.field: Technical/logical, managerial/administrative, physical/environmental, operational. Books often use "administrative" where the exam says "managerial".
Preventive, deterrent, corrective, detective, compensating, directive. Note: "deterrent" and "directive" are not synonymous.

blocks.text: The Six Types, One by One

items: **Preventive**: stops the event. Firewall, MFA, lock, patch.
**Deterrent**: discourages through fear of consequences. Visible camera, warning banner, announced penalties.
**Corrective**: reduces impact after the event. Restoration, rollback, quarantine.
**Detective**: identifies the event. IDS, SIEM, smoke detector, log review.
**Compensating**: replaces an impossible or failing control. Enhanced monitoring of an unpatchable system.
**Directive**: guides behavior. Policy, procedure, "Do Not Enter" sign.

blocks.title: Confusions That Cost Points
blocks.text: A **camera** is deterrent if visible, detective if footage is analyzed. An **IPS** is preventive (it blocks), an **IDS** is detective (it alerts). A **response plan** is directive before the incident, corrective during. The same object changes type depending on use: read the intent described in the scenario.
The Four Categories

**Technical/logical**: implemented in a system (firewall, ACL, encryption). **Managerial/administrative**: defined by a rule or organization (policy, training, separation of duties). **Physical/environmental**: acts on the physical world (badge, mantrap, UPS). **Operational**: tied to daily operations (backup, monitoring, log review, maintenance).

head: Control
Category
Type
Why
rows: Prevents use of a password alone
Sets the rule, does not enforce it

blocks.text: The dual **categories × types** taxonomy is not presented in any of the four books. It is written here for the exam objectives, with verified examples.

blocks.q: A critical system cannot receive a patch. The team adds enhanced network monitoring and a web application firewall in front of the application. How should this control be classified?
blocks.explain: The control compensates for a vulnerability that cannot be patched. It may also be preventive in its mechanics (the WAF blocks), but its **function** in the reasoning is compensating: it replaces the missing patch.

items: Category = nature of the control (technical, managerial, physical, operational).
Type = temporal function (preventive, deterrent, corrective, detective, compensating, directive).
The same control can change type depending on use: the scenario's intent decides.
Knowing how to classify matters more than knowing how to list: the exam tests classification.
